front.title: IPv4 Traffic over an IPv6-Only Segment Routing MPLS Underlay Network

abstract.t: Segment Routing over MPLS (SR-MPLS) can be deployed with an IPv6-only underlay and overlay. In such deployments, the IGP links among Provider (P) and Provider Edge (PE) routers and the BGP sessions between PEs are IPv6-only. The PEs' Prefix-SIDs are bound to IPv6 prefixes, and IPv4 reachability is advertised with IPv6 next hops. This document refers to such deployments as SR-MPLSv6.

This document specifies procedures for network layer awareness in the SR-MPLS data plane when IPv4 packets are carried using a Prefix-SID bound to an IPv6 prefix, without a service label. The procedures address identification of the exposed payload after label removal and selection of the appropriate Explicit NULL label. They cover penultimate hop popping, replacement with Explicit NULL, and ultimate hop popping, without requiring an additional label to identify IPv4 packets.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Segment Routing (SR) over the MPLS data plane (SR-MPLS) is specified in . SR-MPLS can be deployed with an IPv6-only underlay and overlay: the point-to-point IGP links are IPv6-only, the Prefix-SIDs that identify Provider Edge (PE) routers are attached to their IPv6 loopback addresses, and the BGP sessions between PEs are IPv6-only. IPv4 routing is then enabled by advertising IPv4 Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) with IPv6 next hops . This document refers to such a deployment as SR-MPLSv6.

The existing specifications do not define the label-processing procedures for SR-MPLSv6 when IPv4 packets are forwarded in the global routing table, i.e., without a service label. Such packets carry the egress PE's Prefix-SID label, which is bound to an IPv6 prefix. A node that pops this label and exposes the payload, or replaces it with an Explicit NULL label, needs to identify the payload's network layer protocol. Ambiguity in how that protocol is determined can lead to inconsistent forwarding behavior and interoperability problems.

Some implementations use an approach similar to IPv6 Provider Edge (6PE) , in which BGP Labeled Unicast (BGP-LU) , or a similar mechanism, provides an additional bottom-of-stack label to identify IPv4 packets. This label may be the IPv4 Explicit NULL label. This approach increases the required label stack depth. When the IPv4 Explicit NULL label is used, packets using this option arrive at the egress PE with that label, and therefore Penultimate Hop Popping is no longer an option to operators.

Services that use a bottom-of-stack service label, including VRF-based services, are not affected by this ambiguity. The service label determines the forwarding treatment at the egress PE according to the applicable service procedures, as described in .

identifies connecting IPv4 islands over an IPv6-only MPLS network as a major gap. describes IPv4 Provider Edge (4PE) deployment options that address this gap, most of which use the approach described in of this document. For the two single-label options described in its Sections and , that draft notes that deeper packet inspection may be required to identify the network layer protocol, but does not specify the inspection procedure.

This document does not propose the same approach as . It builds more directly on the approach described in for interconnecting IPv4 islands over an IPv6 backbone, in which IPv4 unicast routes are advertised without labels and with IPv6 next hops. The BGP next hop for such a route is the egress PE's IPv6 loopback address. The ingress PE resolves this next hop to the Prefix-SID bound to that address. No additional label is needed to identify IPv4 packets.

This document introduces layer 3 (network layer) awareness into the SR-MPLS data plane. Depending on the network configuration and topology, the first hop, penultimate hop, or ultimate hop inspects the payload's network layer header to determine its address family and applies the corresponding forwarding procedures. describes the problem in detail, specifies these procedures, and illustrates the reference topologies they address.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the terminology of , , and . The IPv4 Explicit NULL label (0), the IPv6 Explicit NULL label (2), and the Implicit NULL label (3) are defined in . In addition, the following terms are used:

dl.dd: An SR-MPLS deployment in which the IGP underlay (point-to-point links and Prefix-SIDs) and the BGP overlay sessions between PEs are IPv6-only, and IPv4 reachability is provided by advertising IPv4 NLRI with IPv6 next hops . SR-MPLSv6 uses the MPLS data plane; it is distinct from Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) .
The ingress PE, which receives a packet from a Customer Edge (CE) router, imposes the Prefix-SID label of the egress PE (the PUSH operation of ), and forwards the packet into the SR-MPLS domain.
A Label Switching Router (LSR) that swaps the Prefix-SID label (the CONTINUE operation of ).
The upstream neighbor of the Prefix-SID originator along the path of the packet, i.e., the node immediately before the ultimate hop.
The egress PE, which originates the Prefix-SID attached to its IPv6 loopback address and is the BGP next hop of the IPv4 route.
The network layer protocol (IPv4 or IPv6) of the packet carried beneath the label stack. This is distinct from the address family of the prefix to which the Prefix-SID is bound.

section.t: For the PE-to-PE forwarding paths described in this document, the first hop is the ingress PE, and the ultimate hop is the egress PE. These terms describe path positions and provider-edge roles, respectively.

section.name: Problem Statement
section.t: This section describes the payload-identification and forwarding issues that arise when IPv4 packets are carried over SR-MPLSv6 without a service label. It also describes existing workarounds and cases that are unaffected.

section.name: Identifying the Network Layer Protocol of the Payload
section.t: The MPLS label stack does not contain any field that explicitly identifies the network layer protocol of the payload. Instead, the network layer protocol must be inferable from the value of the label that is popped from the bottom of the stack, possibly along with the contents of the network layer header itself (). Accordingly, the label initially pushed onto a network layer packet must be associated either with a single network layer protocol or with a specified set of protocols distinguishable by inspecting the network layer header. Any label value that replaces this label in transit must satisfy the same criteria.

In SR-MPLSv6, the ingress PE resolves an IPv4 route whose BGP next hop is the IPv6 loopback address of the egress PE , and imposes the Prefix-SID label that is bound to that IPv6 address. That label is therefore bound to an IPv6 prefix, but carries an IPv4 packet and has the S bit set. Neither nor the IGP extensions for Segment Routing state whether such a label may carry IPv4 packets, nor how a node that pops or swaps the label determines the network layer protocol of the packet beneath it.

section.name: Penultimate Hop Popping
section.t: When the Prefix-SID is advertised with the P-Flag (No-PHP) clear, the penultimate hop pops the corresponding label (). If this operation empties the label stack, forwarding the exposed packet to the ultimate hop requires the penultimate hop to identify its network layer protocol and select the appropriate link-layer protocol identifier, such as the EtherType on an Ethernet link.

In SR-MPLSv6, the exposed packet may be IPv4, while the outgoing interface is an IPv6-only IGP adjacency towards the ultimate hop. The IGP provides IPv6 reachability to the ultimate hop, but this does not by itself establish support for transmitting an unlabeled IPv4 packet over the associated outgoing adjacency.

The mechanisms specified for integrated IS-IS , multi-topology IS-IS , and OSPFv3 address families do not define IPv4 routing through IPv6 next hops comparable to the capability provided by for BGP, as discussed in . Support for both address families within an IGP therefore does not imply support for IPv4-via-IPv6 forwarding.

PHP forwarding uses the next hop selected by the label lookup (). It therefore does not inherently require an IPv4 route to the packet's destination at the penultimate hop. Nevertheless, the forwarding implementation must support transmitting the exposed IPv4 packet over the selected outgoing adjacency, even when the outgoing interface has only IPv6 addressing. If the implementation does not support this operation, the packet is discarded at the penultimate hop.

section.name: Explicit NULL
section.t: For IS-IS, when the Prefix-SID is advertised with both the P-Flag and the E-Flag set, the penultimate hop replaces the corresponding label with an Explicit NULL label, with a value of "0 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6" (Sections and of ). specifies the corresponding behavior for OSPFv3. These specifications do not explicitly state whether the value is selected according to the address family of the advertised prefix or according to the network layer protocol of the packet being forwarded.

If the value is selected according to the address family of the prefix to which the Prefix-SID is bound, the IPv4 packet is sent to the ultimate hop with the IPv6 Explicit NULL label. That label specifies that, after it is popped, forwarding is based on the IPv6 header (). The label therefore identifies the payload as IPv6 even though the packet is IPv4. This mismatch may cause the ultimate hop to discard the packet.

section.name: Existing Workarounds
section.t: An ingress PE can avoid the ambiguity by imposing an additional bottom-of-stack label that identifies the packet as IPv4, analogous to the second level of labels used by 6PE (). That label can be advertised by the egress PE using BGP-LU , as described in , and can be the IPv4 Explicit NULL label.

This approach requires BGP-LU, or an equivalent mechanism, in addition to or instead of plain IPv4 unicast NLRI. The additional label consumes one entry in the label stack solely to identify the payload as IPv4. On hardware with limited label imposition capacity (see Maximum SID Depth ), this leaves fewer entries available for other labels and can restrict the segment lists that the ingress PE can impose.

section.name: Unaffected Cases
section.t: Services in which the bottom-of-stack label is a service label, such as BGP/MPLS IP VPNs , are not affected by the ambiguity described above. For such services, the Prefix-SID label is not at the bottom of the stack. Removing it therefore leaves a labeled packet rather than exposing the network layer header. The service label determines the subsequent forwarding treatment at the egress PE according to the applicable service procedures.
IPv6 packets carried over a Prefix-SID bound to an IPv6 prefix are not affected either.

section.name: Network Layer Awareness
section.t: This section specifies procedures for network layer awareness in the SR-MPLS data plane. In terms of , a Prefix-SID label that is bound to an IPv6 prefix in an SR-MPLSv6 deployment is used for the set of network layer protocols consisting of IPv4 and IPv6, and packets of the two protocols are distinguished by inspection of the network layer header as specified in .

The procedures apply to packets that are forwarded using a Prefix-SID that is bound to an IPv6 prefix of the egress PE, and that carry no label beneath that Prefix-SID, i.e., the Prefix-SID label has the S bit set when it is popped or replaced. Packets with additional labels beneath the Prefix-SID are processed as specified in and are not affected by this document.
Depending on the configuration of the Prefix-SID, i.e., the P-Flag and the E-Flag , the payload address family is determined by the penultimate hop (Sections and ) or by the ultimate hop ().

section.name: Determining the Payload Address Family
section.t: A node determines the payload address family by inspecting the Version field, i.e., the first four bits, of the network layer header that immediately follows the label stack entry with the S bit set. The value 4 indicates IPv4 , and the value 6 indicates IPv6 .
If the Version field contains any other value, the node MUST NOT apply the procedures in this document, and MUST process the packet as it would in the absence of this document.
Inspection of the first nibble beyond the label stack is already commonly performed by LSRs, e.g., for equal-cost multipath (ECMP) load balancing .

section.name: Implicit NULL
section.t: This procedure applies when the Prefix-SID of the ultimate hop is advertised with the P-Flag clear, i.e., when the penultimate hop pops the Prefix-SID.

The ingress PE receives an IPv4 packet whose route resolves to the IPv6 /128 loopback address of the egress PE. The ingress PE and the transit nodes apply the PUSH and CONTINUE operations as specified in , until the packet reaches the penultimate hop.
When the penultimate hop pops the Prefix-SID and the label stack becomes empty, the penultimate hop MUST determine the payload address family as specified in .

ul.li: If the payload is IPv4, the penultimate hop MUST transmit the packet to the ultimate hop as an IPv4 packet. On an Ethernet link, this means that the penultimate hop sets the EtherType to 0x0800 and sends the frame to the link-layer address of the ultimate hop.
If the payload is IPv6, the penultimate hop MUST transmit the packet to the ultimate hop as an IPv6 packet, e.g., with EtherType 0x86DD on an Ethernet link.

section.t: The ultimate hop thereby receives the packet with a link-layer protocol identifier that matches its network layer header, and processes it for further routing or switching like any other native IPv4 or IPv6 packet.

section.name: Explicit NULL
section.t: This procedure applies when the Prefix-SID of the ultimate hop is advertised with both the P-Flag and the E-Flag set, i.e., when the penultimate hop replaces the Prefix-SID with an Explicit NULL label ().

The ingress PE and the transit nodes behave as described in . When the penultimate hop replaces a Prefix-SID label that has the S bit set with an Explicit NULL label, it MUST determine the payload address family as specified in , and MUST select the Explicit NULL label according to the payload address family rather than according to the address family of the prefix to which the Prefix-SID is bound:

ul.li: If the payload is IPv4, the penultimate hop MUST use the IPv4 Explicit NULL label (0).
If the payload is IPv6, the penultimate hop MUST use the IPv6 Explicit NULL label (2).

section.t: The penultimate hop then forwards the packet to the ultimate hop using the regular IGP forwarding procedures. The ultimate hop thereby receives the packet with the Explicit NULL label that matches the payload, and processes the packet for further routing or switching in its global routing table as specified in .

section.name: First Hop and Ultimate Hop
section.t: The first hop knows the address family of each packet that it receives from a CE. When the first hop is itself the penultimate hop, i.e., when the first hop and the ultimate hop are adjacent, it produces the result of or without inspecting the packet: it transmits an IPv4 packet without a label and with the IPv4 link-layer protocol identifier (implicit NULL), or imposes only the IPv4 Explicit NULL label (explicit NULL).

When the Prefix-SID is advertised with the P-Flag set and the E-Flag clear, the penultimate hop keeps the Prefix-SID on top of the stack (), and the ultimate hop pops it. The action of the ultimate hop after popping a label depends on the instruction associated with the label and on the contents of the packet underneath (); the ultimate hop determines the payload address family as specified in and processes the packet accordingly.

t.cref: The procedures for the first hop and the ultimate hop are to be completed. This includes whether an ultimate hop should accept an IPv4 packet received with the IPv6 Explicit NULL label from a penultimate hop that does not implement this document.

section.name: Example Topologies
section.t: The topologies in this section illustrate SR-MPLSv6 deployments that the procedures in this document need to account for. In each, the core runs IS-IS over IPv6-only point-to-point links, the Prefix-SIDs are attached to the IPv6 loopback addresses of the PEs, and the PEs exchange IPv4 and IPv6 routes over IPv6-only iBGP sessions, with IPv4 NLRI carried as specified in . The addressing and protocols used in both topologies are summarized in .

t.cref: Behavior in both the ECMP and the non-ECMP cases needs verification.

section.t: In , IPv4 traffic from CE1 to CE2 enters the SR-MPLS domain at PE1, which imposes the Prefix-SID of the IPv6 loopback address of PE2. P1 and P2 provide equal-cost paths, and whichever of them forwards a given packet acts as the penultimate hop.

section.name: Deployment
section.t: The procedures in and are performed by the penultimate hop, which is not the node that imposes the Prefix-SID. A first hop therefore cannot, by itself, ensure that IPv4 packets are delivered correctly. Every node that can act as the penultimate hop for the Prefix-SID of an egress PE, including nodes on ECMP paths and on fast-reroute repair paths, needs to implement this document. In , for example, PE4 becomes the penultimate hop for traffic to PE3 if both links between PE3 and the P routers fail.

In a network in which some nodes do not implement this document, IPv4 traffic can be discarded. Operators can avoid this by ensuring that all potential penultimate hops implement this document before carrying IPv4 traffic without an additional label, or by continuing to use one of the approaches described in towards egress PEs for which this cannot be ensured.

t.cref: A capability advertisement, e.g., an IGP flag, that would allow an ingress PE to determine whether the penultimate hops towards an egress PE implement this document is for further study.

section.name: IPv4 Packets on IPv6-Only Links
section.t: With the procedure in , the ultimate hop receives native IPv4 packets on core-facing interfaces that have no IPv4 address. The penultimate hop resolves the link-layer address of the ultimate hop using IPv6 Neighbor Discovery , so neither an IPv4 address nor ARP is needed on the link. The ultimate hop, however, needs to accept and process IPv4 packets received on such interfaces; implementations that discard IPv4 packets received on interfaces on which IPv4 is not enabled need IPv4 processing to be enabled on the core-facing interfaces of the ultimate hop.

section.name: Label Stack Depth
section.t: Compared to the approaches described in , the procedures in this document carry IPv4 packets with one label fewer. This is beneficial where the Maximum SID Depth of the ingress PE limits the number of labels that can be imposed.

section.name: Equal-Cost Multipath
section.t: Transit nodes commonly inspect the first nibble beyond the label stack to select among ECMP paths . This document does not change that behavior. As noted in , behavior in both the ECMP and the non-ECMP cases needs verification.

When Entropy Labels are used, the Prefix-SID is not at the bottom of the label stack. A penultimate hop may, however, pop the Entropy Label Indicator and the Entropy Label in addition to the Prefix-SID (), which exposes the payload in the same way as described in . The interaction of this document with Entropy Labels is an open issue ().

section.name: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance
section.t: LSRs that run IPv6 only cannot generate ICMPv4 messages for IPv4 packets whose TTL expires within the SR-MPLS domain (); this document does not address that gap. LSP Ping and Traceroute for SR-MPLS validate the Prefix-SID itself, but do not exercise the procedures in this document; operators may need to complement them with end-to-end IPv4 probes.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document does not introduce any new control plane messages or extensions, and the security considerations of , , and apply.

notes that SR does not introduce any new behavior in the MPLS data plane. This document does introduce a data plane behavior: the penultimate hop, and in some cases the ultimate hop, inspects the first four bits of the network layer header that follows the label stack entry with the S bit set. That inspection is at a fixed offset and of a fixed size, and is comparable to the inspection that LSRs already perform for ECMP . Packets whose Version field is neither 4 nor 6 are processed as they would be in the absence of this document.

The procedures allow IPv4 packets that carry only a Prefix-SID to be delivered into the global routing table of the egress PE. This is not a new capability: a node that can inject labeled packets into the SR domain can already achieve the same result by imposing an IPv4 Explicit NULL label beneath the Prefix-SID. As with any SR-MPLS deployment, SR domain boundary routers are required to filter external traffic destined to labels associated with segments within the trusted domain ().

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: The following issues are open and are to be resolved in future revisions of this document:

ol.li: Whether this document updates , , and with respect to the selection of the Explicit NULL label value ().

Whether a capability advertisement is needed so that an ingress PE can determine that the penultimate hops towards an egress PE implement this document (); such an advertisement would require IANA actions.
Completion of the procedures for the first hop and the ultimate hop ().
Verification of behavior in both the ECMP and the non-ECMP cases of the example topologies ().
Interaction with Entropy Labels , including a penultimate hop that pops the Entropy Label along with the Prefix-SID (), and with fast-reroute repair paths.
Whether the procedures should also apply to IPv6 payloads carried over Prefix-SIDs bound to IPv4 prefixes, and to IPv6-signaled LDP LSPs .
Whether the procedures are enabled by default or only by configuration.
